partner_context.their_ambition: The West Bengal Transport Corporation moves hundreds of thousands of commuters a day across the Hooghly — the river crossings that keep Kolkata and Howrah connected while the Howrah Bridge and the city's roads sit at a standstill. WBTC's ambition is a faster, cleaner, more reliable public ferry network, and it has already put India's first next-generation electric ferry on the water to get there.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the foiling-electric upgrade to a network WBTC already runs every day. The same crossings — Howrah to central Kolkata, the northern ghats, the pilgrimage riverfront, the upriver heritage towns — flown clear of the water: faster, near-silent, low-wake and zero-emission, on the ghats and jetties that already exist.

hero.eyebrow: Authority proposal · Kolkata, India · West Bengal Transport Corporation
hero.title: Navier × Kolkata Ferries — the Hooghly, on foils
hero.subtitle: A zero-emission foiling layer on the Kolkata–Howrah crossings and the Hooghly riverfront: faster commutes, cleaner air, and real relief for one of India's most congested cores.
hero.what_we_do_together: WBTC brings the Hooghly ferry network, the ghats and the public-service mandate; Navier brings the foiling-electric fleet, captain training and certification path. Together we run the same river the city depends on — faster, quieter and zero-emission — extending the electric-ferry program West Bengal has already begun.

why_now: West Bengal has moved first: 'Dheu', a next-generation battery-electric ferry, was delivered in January 2025 and is already carrying passengers on the Hooghly, with 13 more hybrid-electric vessels under construction for the state. The market pull and the political will exist today — a foiling-electric layer is the fast, low-wake next step.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the existing Hooghly ferry network — Howrah Ferry Ghat beside Howrah station, the central ghats at Fairlie Place and Millennium Park, the northern riverfront and the pilgrimage jetties at Dakshineswar and Belur Math — taking the high-frequency commuter and riverfront crossings while conventional vessels keep heavier runs. Commuters step from suburban rail and metro straight onto a foil across the river.

differentiation.why_navier: The platform is proven in service and purpose-built for exactly this job: 10x more efficient than a planing hull, low-wake (critical on a busy, erosion-prone river), near-silent, and zero-emission. It extends West Bengal's live electric-ferry program to the fast crossings where speed and wake have kept diesel in service longest.

objections.concern: Can an electric fleet handle a busy, silt-laden river like the Hooghly?
objections.response: Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at the existing ghats, flies above the chop and wake for a smoother ride, and its low wake reduces bank erosion on a heavily-used river — an advantage, not a liability, in these conditions.

objections.concern: Is this affordable for a public network?
objections.response: Foiling-electric is ~10x more efficient than a diesel planing hull, so fuel — the largest operating cost — falls sharply; the same public budget runs more frequent crossings.

objections.concern: Does this replace the ferries people rely on?
objections.response: No — it's a faster layer above them. Conventional ferries keep running underneath; the foiling fleet adds speed and zero-emission capacity on the busiest crossings.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling-electric fleet, captain training, and the maintenance and certification path, aligned to Indian Register of Shipping battery-vessel guidelines.
the_ask.partner_brings: The Hooghly ferry route map, the ghats and jetties, the public-service mandate, and the phased fleet-modernization plan already underway.
the_ask.next_step: Identify the first Kolkata–Howrah crossing for a foiling-electric public pilot and align it with WBTC's electric-ferry rollout.

close.body: West Bengal has already put the first electric ferry on the Hooghly. Navier is how that program reaches the busiest crossings fastest — giving every commuter a quick, quiet, zero-emission ride across the river, and giving one of India's most congested cities real relief on the water.
